title: Best Speech-to-Text for Noisy Audio in 2026: What Holds Up on Real Phone Calls
summary: The best speech-to-text for noisy audio, measured: how 30+ STT models hold up on clipped, distant, phone-compressed, and accented speech. See the results.
body_markdown:
The accuracy score you picked your model on was probably earned on clean speech read into a good microphone, but your callers are messier. They ring in on speakerphone from the car, press the phone against their mouth, speak with accents, and reach your agent through a phone network that compresses every word. OpenAI’s[GPT Realtime Whisper](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-realtime-whisper) shows what that can cost. In our benchmark, its[word error rate](https://www.coval.ai/blog/word-error-rate-stt-2026/) (WER, the share of words a transcript gets wrong) goes from 4.1% on clean speech to 15.9% on the same sentences once they’re clipped, the distortion you hear when a voice is too loud for the microphone.


Picking the best speech-to-text for noisy audio comes down to knowing which of those conditions a model survives. So we ran 30+ models through each one.


> **Quick answer:** AssemblyAI’s[Universal 3.6 Pro](https://www.assemblyai.com/blog/universal-3-6-pro-realtime) is the most accurate speech-to-text model on messy phone audio in[our benchmarks](https://benchmarks.coval.ai/stt) , with a word error rate of 2.6% to 3.3% from clean speech through clipped, distant, and phone-compressed audio, and 2.0% on accented English. Universal 3.5 Pro is a close second, tied with it on clipped audio at 3.1%. The strongest pick from another provider is Alibaba’s Qwen3 ASR Fast, third on clipped audio at 5.4%. Clipping is what separates models: 20 of 30 made more than 5 extra errors per 100 words on clipped audio, while phone compression alone added fewer than 2 for 23 of them (30-day averages as of Nov 4, 2026).


The lesson under the picks is that one average score hides the condition that breaks your agent, so choose on the conditions your callers bring. The scorecard comes first, then each condition in turn, then accented English, why a single leaderboard number misses all this, and how to test on calls that sound like yours.


## The best speech-to-text for noisy audio: how 10 models score under each condition


Every number here comes from our[speech-to-text benchmark](https://benchmarks.coval.ai/datasets) , which runs 30+ models on the same audio and reports a 30-day average for each. The audio comes from[WildASR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.25727) , a benchmark from Boson AI that takes real recordings of people reading English sentences and degrades them one condition at a time. Our[clean set](https://benchmarks.coval.ai/datasets/stt-wildasr-clean) is 284 of those recordings, untouched. Each degraded set is the same 284 with one call problem applied: a caller who’s too loud (clipping), a caller across the room (far-field), bursts of noise and silence between words (noise gaps), or a phone network’s compression (phone codec). The sentences never change, so any rise in errors comes from the condition, not from harder sentences.


Here are ten of those models, sorted by clean WER. Each cell is the model’s WER under that condition, with its rise over the clean score in parentheses, in percentage points (one point is one extra error per 100 words).

Universal 3.6 Pro has the lowest WER in every column, tied with Universal 3.5 Pro on clipping and noise gaps, and both AssemblyAI Pro models stay within a point of their clean score under every condition. Universal 3.6 Pro is the more accurate of the two, but Universal 3.5 Pro is the steadier: it rises less on clipping, noise gaps, and the phone codec, and matches it on far-field. Qwen3 ASR Fast is the steadiest of the rest: third in every column above, and nearly flat on noise gaps.


A vendor’s newer model can hold up where its older one doesn’t. AssemblyAI’s older[Universal Streaming](https://benchmarks.coval.ai/models/universal-streaming) rose 11.7 points on the same clipped recordings where Universal 3.6 Pro rose 0.5. In its[launch post](https://www.assemblyai.com/blog/universal-3-6-pro-realtime) , AssemblyAI says it trained 3.6 Pro on “tens of thousands of hours of real voice-agent and telephony conversations.”


Read down the columns instead, and you see which conditions cost accuracy at all.


## Clipping does the most damage, and the phone codec barely registers


Loudness and distance are what pull models apart. Noise between words and phone compression barely move most of them.


### Clipping: a caller who is too loud


Clipping happens when a voice is too loud for the microphone or the audio path, so the loudest peaks get flattened. Think of a caller shouting, or holding the phone right against their mouth. WildASR[flattens the top 40%](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.25727v1) of each recording’s amplitude values.


This is where the leaderboard splits. On our[clipping set](https://benchmarks.coval.ai/datasets/stt-wildasr-clipping) , only the two AssemblyAI Pro models added less than a point. Google’s[Gemini 3.5 Transcribe Live](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-3-5-transcribe/) rose 7.4 points, ElevenLabs’[Scribe v2 Realtime](https://elevenlabs.io/blog/introducing-scribe-v2-realtime) 7.9, and GPT Realtime Whisper 11.8. At the bottom of the board, NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 ASR Streaming rose 29.4 points.


Models that sit within a few points of each other on clean speech spread far apart once the same 284 sentences are clipped. Source: Coval speech-to-text benchmark, WildASR clean and clipping sets, 30-day averages as of Nov 4, 2026.


### Far-field: a caller across the room


Far-field audio is speech picked up from a distance, like a speakerphone on a desk or a phone lying on the car seat. WildASR simulates a room and places the microphone[4, 8, or 16 meters](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.25727v1) from the speaker. On our[far-field set](https://benchmarks.coval.ai/datasets/stt-wildasr-farfield) , five models rose 0.7 points or less: Inworld’s STT 1 (+0.4), both AssemblyAI Pro models, Qwen3 ASR Fast, and Qwen3 ASR 1.7b. GPT Realtime Whisper rose 5.5 points, and the largest rise on the board was 12.2, for Gradium’s Default model.


### Noise gaps: a call that cuts in and out


Noise gaps are bursts of noise and stretches of silence inserted between bits of speech, so every clip runs longer than its clean version. The noise fills the pauses rather than sitting under the words, and the set tests whether transcription[recovers after an interruption](https://benchmarks.coval.ai/datasets/stt-wildasr-noisegap) . Most models handle it well. Every model on the board rose 6.1 points or less, and 14 of 30 rose 1.3 or less. Qwen3 ASR Fast barely moved (+0.2), and Universal 3.5 Pro added 0.3.


### Phone codec: the network itself


A codec is the compression a phone network applies to fit a voice into a narrow channel.[WildASR runs](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.25727v1) each clip through GSM, the classic mobile standard, or G.711 μ-law, the standard for landlines and VoIP. Both squeeze the audio down to 8 kHz and back. Most models barely notice. On our[phone codec set](https://benchmarks.coval.ai/datasets/stt-wildasr-phonecodec) , the largest rise on the whole board was 3.4 points. Universal 3.6 Pro moved 0.1, Google’s[Chirp 3](https://cloud.google.com/speech-to-text/v2/docs/chirp_3-model) moved 0.2, and Qwen3 ASR Fast didn’t move at all.


So the phone line on its own isn’t what wrecks a transcript. A caller who is too loud or too far from the phone is, and those are the two conditions to test your shortlist on hardest.


## Accented English: Universal 3.6 Pro leads a widely spread field


Universal 3.6 Pro is also the most accurate model on accented English, at 2.0%. Our[accent set](https://benchmarks.coval.ai/datasets/stt-wildasr-accent) is a separate test: 845 clips of English from speakers with a[wide range of accents](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.25727v1) , including Canadian, Australian, and German. Because the speakers and sentences differ from the clean set, these scores compare models with each other, not with their clean results.


The five most accurate models on accented English:


Model WER on accented English


Universal 3.6 Pro (AssemblyAI) 2.0%


[Realtime Global](https://benchmarks.coval.ai/models/realtime-global) (Reson8) 2.5%


[resonant-1](https://benchmarks.coval.ai/models/realtime) (Reson8) 2.6%


Universal 3.5 Pro (AssemblyAI) 2.8%


Qwen3 ASR Fast (Alibaba) 2.9%


The rest of the scorecard models land between 3.8% for Gemini 3.5 Transcribe Live and 6.9% for Deepgram’s[Flux](https://developers.deepgram.com/changelog/2025/10/2) , with GPT Realtime Whisper at 5.4%. That’s a wide spread: the least accurate model in our scorecard makes more than three times as many errors on accented speech as the most accurate.


## Why one WER score hides the condition that breaks your agent


Rank on clean audio doesn’t carry over to bad audio, so a single leaderboard number can’t tell you which model will hold up for your callers. Gemini 3.5 Transcribe Live is third of 30 on clean speech and 11th on clipped audio. Speechmatics’ Linden 1 goes the other way, from 16th on clean to seventh on clipped. Universal 3.5 Pro and Gemini 3.5 Transcribe Live sit 0.2 points apart on clean speech and 7.3 points apart once the audio clips.


The WildASR authors found the same pattern in the systems they tested, concluding that models “[can excel on standard benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.25727v1) yet fail drastically under real-world conditions.” That’s why each of our dataset pages charts every model’s rise over the clean baseline, condition by condition.


Bad audio doesn’t slow transcription down, so latency won’t flag the problem. Universal 3.6 Pro’s final transcript arrived 102 to 113 ms after the speaker stopped talking on every one of our[test sets](https://benchmarks.coval.ai/models/universal-3.6-pro) , and Deepgram’s[Nova 3](https://deepgram.com/learn/introducing-nova-3-speech-to-text-api) held between 84 and 95 ms. What bad audio changes is accuracy, and you only see that by measuring accuracy under each condition.


## How we measured it


The clean set is 284 English sentences read aloud, drawn from FLEURS, a public read-speech dataset. Boson AI explains how WildASR builds each condition in its March 2026 paper,[Back to Basics: Revisiting ASR in the Age of Voice Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.25727) , and the audio is public on[Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/bosonai/WildASR) .


We run every model through our[open-source benchmark runner](https://github.com/coval-ai/benchmarks) from the us-east-1 region, and each run draws one sample of clips that all models share. Before scoring, Whisper’s EnglishTextNormalizer, the de facto standard for published WER, evens out formatting like capitals and punctuation. WER is then corpus-level: errors summed across all clips, divided by all the words spoken. Every figure here is a 30-day average. The full method is in our[methodology notes](https://github.com/coval-ai/benchmarks/blob/main/docs/methodology.md) .


## Test the conditions your callers bring


The benchmark tells you which models to shortlist. It can’t play your callers. WildASR’s noise fills the pauses, but your callers’ TV, car, or open-plan office plays under every word, and your accent mix isn’t the benchmark’s. Nor can a WER chart tell you whether a misheard account number cost you the call, which is the error that matters.


That’s what Coval’s[simulations](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/simulations/overview) are for. In a simulation, Coval plays a realistic caller, talks to your agent end to end, and scores the conversation against criteria you define. Each simulated caller is a[persona](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/personas/overview) , which sets the caller’s voice, language and accent, audio environment, and conversational behavior. You can pick background noise from a built-in library or upload a recording of your own callers’ surroundings. Coval mixes it into the caller’s side of the call at the volume you set and loops it for the whole conversation. Built-in personas such as the High Background Noise Speaker and the Low Volume Speaker[cover common audio problems](https://docs.coval.ai/guides/testing-across-audio-qualities) , and the[accent personas](https://docs.coval.ai/guides/testing-across-accents) include Indian, Nigerian, Malaysian, and US Southern accents.


Then score what matters. The[Transcription Error](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/types/ml-model) metric measures WER on the call itself: it compares the call’s transcript with an independent re-transcription Coval makes from the call recording, so you don’t need to instrument your agent first. An[LLM judge metric](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/types/llm-judge) answers a question you write, such as whether the agent captured the caller’s account number correctly. Run the[same test set](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/agents/mutations) against each speech-to-text vendor on your shortlist, compare the results by persona, and you’ll see which model holds up for your callers and whether its misses cost the call.


Start your shortlist with Universal 3.6 Pro, with Universal 3.5 Pro and Qwen3 ASR Fast behind it (our[speech-to-text provider guide](https://www.coval.ai/blog/best-speech-to-text-providers-in-2026-independent-benchmarks-and-how-to-choose/) covers price and features). Give the most weight to the condition your callers bring most often. Then prove the pick on calls that sound like yours before your callers prove it for you.
